# Innovation {#sec-innovation}

## The learned decision rule {#sec-innovation-rule}

```{python}
#| label: innovation-rule-setup
from pathlib import Path

from ryuk.evaluation.draws import ENROLLED_PER_IDENTITY
from ryuk.evaluation.names import model_name
from ryuk.evaluation.results import read_results

# Quarto runs the kernel in report/, so the committed results are one level up.
rule_results = read_results(Path("../evaluation/results.json"))
assert rule_results is not None and rule_results.learning is not None
rule_learning = rule_results.learning
assert rule_results.identification is not None
rule_gallery = len(rule_results.identification.selection("test").gallery)
rule_compared = {c.model.network: c for c in rule_learning.models}


def rule_model(network: str) -> str:
    return model_name(rule_compared[network].model)


def rule_gain(network: str) -> str:
    """The learned rule's test TPIR gain over best photo for one model, with its interval."""
    measured = rule_compared[network].method("learned").gain
    assert measured is not None

    def signed(difference: float) -> str:
        text = f"{100 * difference:+.2f}"
        return "0.00" if float(text) == 0 else text.replace("-", "\N{MINUS SIGN}")

    return f"{signed(measured.value)} points ({signed(measured.ci.low)} to {signed(measured.ci.high)})"


assert not any(c.method("learned").gain.improves for c in rule_learning.models)
on_mean = [model_name(c.model) for c in rule_learning.models if c.live_rule == "mean"]
assert len(on_mean) == 2
```

Best photo judges a face by one number, its top candidate's match score. The learned decision rule was Ryuk's attempt to use a second: how far the top candidate stands above the runner-up. A face that resembles two persons of interest almost equally is weaker evidence for either than its top score alone suggests, and a face that resembles one far more than anyone else is stronger. The rule is a logistic regression on exactly those two inputs, fitted for each recognition model to tell right top candidates from wrong ones and from strangers, and the model's threshold would be a cut-off on its output.

Three properties made it a candidate for the live monitor where the classifiers of @sec-eval-learning are not. It is gallery-agnostic: it never sees who is enrolled, only two scores about whoever tops the ranking, so enrollment, removal and purge need nothing refitted. It has two inputs, so its whole behaviour is one line that can be drawn and checked (@fig-learned-rules); the number of enrolled photos is deliberately left out, since it is always `{python} ENROLLED_PER_IDENTITY` in evaluation and varies live. And it is cross-fitted: its cut-off is frozen on out-of-fold output from `{python} rule_learning.folds` identity-grouped folds of the validation draw, so no probe's probability comes from a fit that saw its identity.

It did not measurably beat best photo. On the test draw its TPIR gain at FPIR `{python} f"{rule_learning.target_fpir:.0%}"` is `{python} rule_gain("sface")` for `{python} rule_model("sface")`, `{python} rule_gain("arcface")` for `{python} rule_model("arcface")` and `{python} rule_gain("facenet")` for `{python} rule_model("facenet")`, and no interval lies wholly above zero. The simpler mean rule, which fits nothing, did measurably better for `{python} " and ".join(on_mean)`, and runs live on both. The gap mostly separates what best photo's threshold already separates: wrong top candidates sit close to their runner-up, but they also score low (@fig-gap-distributions).

Making the rule pay would take more than refitting it. It was fitted on galleries of `{python} rule_gallery` identities, where a probe's runner-up is the best of `{python} rule_gallery - 1` others. A live watchlist is usually far smaller, so the runner-up tends to score lower and the same face shows a larger gap; frozen as it is, the rule would be expected to accept more readily live than on the draws it was measured on. With one person on the watchlist there is no runner-up at all, and the live monitor takes the gap as 0, the rule's most demanding case. A rule to trust live would have to be fitted and frozen on galleries of the sizes a watchlist actually has, or take the gallery's size as a third input and be shown to hold across it (@sec-limitation-gallery-size).

## Confirmation in the live monitor {#sec-innovation-confirmation}

```{python}
#| label: innovation-confirmation-setup
from ryuk.watchlist.tracker import (
    CONFIRMATION_WINDOW,
    CROP_MARGIN,
    GAP,
    MIN_CONFIRMING_FRAMES,
    WRITE_INTERVAL,
)


def seconds(span) -> str:
    """A span of time as prose gives it: milliseconds under a second, else seconds."""
    total = span.total_seconds()
    return f"{total * 1000:g} ms" if total < 1 else f"{total:g} s"


def a_share(value: float) -> str:
    """A simple fraction in words, for the crop's margin."""
    return {0.25: "a quarter", 0.5: "half"}.get(value, f"{100 * value:g}%")
```

A match is shown in the live monitor the moment it happens, but one frame is weak evidence. A face caught mid-turn, or a passer-by who resembles a person of interest from one angle, can clear the threshold once, and a log of every such frame would bury the operator in false sightings. So a match is logged only once it holds. A person of interest's sighting opens at confirmation: when they have been matched in at least half the frames processed over the last `{python} seconds(CONFIRMATION_WINDOW)`, and in at least `{python} MIN_CONFIRMING_FRAMES` of them however few frames that window holds. The second condition keeps a slow frame rate from confirming on one or two frames. Matches before confirmation are shown but not logged.

A sighting is one person of interest seen continuously, however many frames that covers. It ends once `{python} seconds(GAP)` have passed since their last match, and also when they are removed or purged, when the operator switches the active model and when the live monitor stops; its end time is the last time they were seen. A person who steps out of view for a moment and back stays one sighting, and the same person returning later opens another. The service also ends sightings on a timer, so one ends on time even when no frame arrives, as while the client's tab is hidden, and it writes an open sighting's changes at most `{python} 'once a second' if WRITE_INTERVAL.total_seconds() == 1 else 'once every ' + seconds(WRITE_INTERVAL)`.

Each sighting keeps what is needed to review it later and nothing more: the face crop of its best match, cut from that frame with a margin of `{python} a_share(CROP_MARGIN)` of the box on each side and never the whole frame; the runner-up at that best match, with their match score; and the recognition model and threshold that produced it, since sightings under different models are not comparable. The runner-up is recorded but never shown live beside a face, so the live monitor names only the match. A runner-up who is later purged is cleared from every sighting, their score kept without their name.

The window and the counts are design choices, not measurements: no labelled video was available to measure how often the rule opens a sighting wrongly or late (@sec-limitation-confirmation).

## What purge guarantees {#sec-innovation-purge}

Purge is how the operator erases a person of interest, as distinct from removal, which takes them off the watchlist and can be undone. One `DELETE` request runs one transaction. It first clears the person as runner-up on everyone else's sightings, keeping the score without the name. It then deletes the person, and the database's foreign keys cascade to their enrolled photos, those photos' embeddings under every recognition model, and their sightings with each sighting's face crop. Once it commits, the live monitor's in-memory embeddings are reloaded without the person and their open sighting ends. Either all of it happens or none of it does.

Within the database file nothing of them is left. `secure_delete` overwrites with zeros every page the purge freed, and the content it deleted from pages still in use, and the rollback journal, which held a copy of every page the transaction changed, is truncated when the transaction commits. The tests show this through the service's HTTP surface, as a client would see it. They enrol two people, record a sighting for one whose crop is large enough to span several database pages and a sighting for the other with the first as runner-up, and purge the first with a `DELETE` request. Every row the person owned is then gone, from persons, photos, embeddings and sightings; the other person's sighting keeps the runner-up's score without their name; and neither a sample of the stored photo's bytes nor one of the crop's appears anywhere in the database file or its journal. Further tests check that the purged person is gone from every list and is never matched by the live monitor again, and that a purge which fails to commit leaves the person and their sightings as they were.

What purge cannot reach lies beneath the file: filesystem snapshots, blocks a filesystem wrote the zeros beside rather than over, the blocks the truncated journal freed, the temporary file a large upload passes through, and old bytes an SSD has not yet erased from its flash (@sec-limitation-purge). The guarantee is that a purged face is gone from the application and its files, and the report does not claim more.
